justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely around $515–516 for the underlying asset (which appears to be SPY or a similar broad equity index ETF based on the price range). For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price with only a slight positive bias, reflecting the general tendency for equity markets to drift upward on short horizons when no major catalyst is imminent. The one-week and one-month estimates extend that drift gradually, consistent with a rough annualized return assumption of somewhere in the 5–8% range applied over those shorter windows. The incremental increases are intentionally small because compounding over days and weeks produces only modest expected movement in absolute dollar terms.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility for a broad equity index instrument. For a single day, historical daily moves of roughly 0.5–1% on either side justify a fairly tight band of about $10–11 wide. Over one week, uncertainty compounds and I widened the interval to roughly $40, reflecting the possibility of a 2–4% swing in either direction, consistent with historical weekly volatility. The one-month interval at $80 wide captures the reality that over four to five weeks, cumulative volatility can produce moves of 5–8% or more in either direction even in ordinary market conditions. These widths are grounded in historical realized volatility rather than implied volatility, so they may understate risk if options markets were pricing elevated uncertainty at the time.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. A significant macroeconomic surprise — such as an unexpected inflation print, a Federal Reserve policy shift, or deteriorating labor market data — could easily produce a 3–5% move within a single day, blowing past even the one-week confidence interval. Geopolitical escalations, a credit event in a major financial institution, or an unexpected earnings shock from a heavyweight index constituent could similarly cause outsized moves. On the upside, a dovish Fed pivot or a surprisingly strong economic data release could spark a sharp rally. The one-month interval is most vulnerable to tail risks that are inherently difficult to anticipate, including policy surprises, sudden liquidity dislocations, or exogenous shocks, any of which could render even a wide $80 range insufficient.
